title: Finding Unreachable Objects

content.intro: This lesson introduces finding unreachable objects as part of Recovery, Maintenance, and Migration. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: `git fsck` reports object connectivity and integrity, including some unreachable objects. Treat its output as diagnostic evidence and preserve the repository before cleanup; it is not a guaranteed repair operation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** `git fsck` reports object connectivity and integrity, including some unreachable objects. Treat its output as diagnostic evidence and preserve the repository before cleanup; it is not a guaranteed repair operation.

For **Finding Unreachable Objects**, keep the named subtopics in view: Reachable versus unreachable objects; Dangling commits and blobs; Understanding object inspection output; Assessing potential recovery candidates. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Do not delete any reported object until you understand whether it is needed for recovery. fsck reports are evidence, not an automatic repair.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
